title: The City Test: Pull, Push, and the Policy Gap
intro: Who moves, what the city demands, and the gap no government owns.

terms.def: The missing design for city Aboriginal services, which no government clearly owns, leaving needs unmet.
The 2003 federal pilot program funding city-level Aboriginal service projects in eight major cities.

body: The move to town is the chapter's biggest number story. Urbanization climbs steadily since the 1940s: of 976,305 Canadians identifying as Aboriginal in 2001, about half lived in cities, with First Nations split 47 percent on reserve, 24 percent urban, 29 percent rural off-reserve, Métis 68 percent urban, and Inuit 10 percent outside the Arctic, most in Yellowknife, Montreal, Ottawa, or Edmonton. Blackfoot keeps the reasons in its vocabulary, with distinct words for living, working, schooling, or waiting outside. The draw runs from schools and clinics to excitement and escape, but the top motives are concrete: housing plus education, training, and jobs. Many shuttle back and forth as work shifts; some return for good missing family.

The city charges six tolls: alien atmosphere, high costs, isolation, hard-to-reach services, strained identity, and the old barriers in new streets. Unemployment runs five to six times the non-Aboriginal rate in the same city, blamed on training, schooling, discrimination, and clashing corporate values, while low-skill wages trap workers: 28 percent of off-reserve Aboriginal people fell below the poverty line in 2001 against 13 percent of non-Aboriginal people. Hope wears young faces, median age 24.7 against 37.7, birth rates half again as high, a third of the population fourteen or under, a coming skilled-labour shortage they could fill, and Edmonton already dropping Aboriginal unemployment from 22 to 13 percent between 1996 and 2001. Elizabeth Métis Settlement's Wilfred Collins states the bet: a hard-working people, once positioned to prove it, become an asset viewed as one.

Services are where the city fails hardest. Urban Aboriginal people get less federal help than reserve or Inuit-community residents, provincial and municipal offerings arrive uncoordinated and uneven, and each order of government points at the other, Ottawa claiming only reserves, Inuit, and northern Métis while provinces claim Ottawa owns every Aboriginal file. Treaty members feel it directly: free addictions treatment on reserve, ineligibility in Edmonton. Add the tax irony, urban members pay income and property tax yet receive less, stretched chiefs and councils triaging local needs first despite the Siksika Calgary office model, and administrators spending more hours chasing grants than clients. Ottawa's 2003 answer, the Urban Aboriginal Strategy, put $25 million over three years into pilots across Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary, Saskatoon, Regina, Winnipeg, Thunder Bay, and Toronto.

Identity frays where supports vanish: no land underfoot, no Elders next door, no ceremonies or languages in the air. The Royal Commission heard that holding identity is essential to urban happiness, yet city demands rewrite values daily, so some commute home constantly while others invent new urban roots. Chapter Five's lesson returns sharpened: education breaks barriers, and nowhere matters more than inside service institutions. Then comes the gap in numbers: 90 percent of federal Aboriginal spending serves reserves, reaching only 47 percent of First Nations and about 30 percent of all Aboriginal people, while policy debates circle treaties, self-government, reserve housing, and claims that barely touch cities. Urban people stay politically unorganized and out of the rooms, even self-government rooms, though Phil Fontaine promises an Assembly of First Nations reinvented to represent Toronto and Winnipeg as fully as Onion Lake. Tsuu T'ina Elders Vera Marie Crowchild and Regina Noel, voicing grandmother Daisy Otter, warn what the vacuum costs: a city plan meant to dissolve treaty obligations, torment instead of welcome, and alcohol filling the void.

example.title: Do the gap math
example.text: Write the two numbers side by side: 90 percent of federal Aboriginal dollars to reserves, 30 percent of Aboriginal people reached. Every urban service you meet for the rest of this theme is a footnote to that subtraction.

check.prompt: Explain the urban policy gap in two numbers.
check.sample: Sample response: about 90 percent of federal Aboriginal spending goes to reserve programming, yet only about 30 percent of all Aboriginal people benefit, leaving the urban majority in a jurisdictional limbo.

title: Friendship Centres and Success Stories
intro: The referral network that became a cultural base, and the people who prove cities workable.

terms.def: An urban hub run by volunteers from the 1950s onward, growing into a referral network and a cultural base for city life.
A lived sense of who your people are, which urban Aboriginal people call essential to happiness and hard to hold.

body: Friendship Centres began as neighbourliness with a card file. As First Nations and Métis migration quickened through the 1950s, local volunteers opened referral desks connecting newcomers to housing, jobs, and services; the 1960s crowds forced expansion into a network with provincial and territorial associations, Alberta's incorporating in 1970 and Ottawa funding all forty centres by 1972. Numbers have more than doubled since, and services outgrew referrals into culture itself. The youth-leader story condenses the arc: a Ginoogaming teen joins Thunder Bay's Li'l Beavers, wins a board youth seat at eighteen in 2000, moves to Edmonton in 2002, and climbs onto the Alberta executive and the national Aboriginal Youth Council, growing up inside the movement.

Success stories answer the deficit file with proper nouns. Matthew Coon Come reached the Assembly of First Nations from a northern Quebec trapline; Joan Beatty reached Saskatchewan's cabinet from Deschambault Lake, where she learned no English until ten, by way of CBC reporting; Tomson Highway carried Cree from a Manitoba trapline onto world stages; George Leach builds a Toronto music career with a Nikita role while fasting and listening to the lake back in Sta'atl'imx Lillooet, insisting he needs both societies; Madawaska Maliseet John Bernard built Ottawa's Donna Cona into a $12 million systems firm, half Aboriginal staff at $60,000 starts, wiring Nunavut's IT and beaming satellite internet to reserves, while his sister stays happily on top of the world back home; Tsuu T'ina ventriloquist Derrick Starlight tours from a Calgary base with his own company and TV slot.

The talking circle turns stories into assignments. Youth weigh their duties to their people, the urbanization trend's future, and which problems bite deepest, against the Royal Commission testimony that daily racism in stores and streets does the worst damage of all, shredding esteem and confidence. Culture answers as safety net: protect urban Aboriginal culture the way Canada protects its own against American flood, because communities without history, tradition, and ceremony lose their strength, while shared activities rebuild the relationships isolated people lean on.

Identity is the thread tying centres to stories. Every success above holds two memberships at once, city professional and community member, and every centre exists so newcomers need not choose. For the Attawapiskat report, widen the evidence table: beside each service row, note whether delivery strengthens or starves identity, because the report's best paragraphs will argue services and culture together.

example.title: Run the interview
example.text: Find one Aboriginal person linking a rural community and city work, and ask the chapter's questions: challenges, benefits, and what held their identity. One quoted sentence from a real interview outweighs a paragraph of summary.

check.prompt: What makes Friendship Centres work where outside programs fail?
check.sample: Sample response: they pair referrals with a cultural base run by the community itself, so help arrives with heritage and identity instead of against it, which is why users report overwhelming satisfaction.
